source_refs.note: Chapter 5 exercise (PDF 113-116), solved: 13 MCQs keyed from the chapter (no key is printed), 13 short and 5 descriptive questions with model answers, 2 numericals worked step by step. MCQ I and V, short f, Q.4 and Q.7 carry Book corrections.

blocks.text: Q.1 Four choices are given for each question. Select the correct choice.

blocks.prompt: I. London dispersion forces are the only forces present among:

options.text: molecules of water in liquid state
atoms of helium in gaseous state at high temperature

blocks.explanation: I₂ is a non-polar molecule, so only London dispersion (id-id) forces hold solid iodine together; they are strong because I₂ is large (iodine is a solid, b.p. 458 K). Water has hydrogen bonds and HCl has dipole-dipole forces. In a gas at high temperature the forces are negligible (the gas behaves ideally, 5.1).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Strictly, helium atoms (b) also have only London dispersion forces, so two options are true. The intended answer is (c): in hot gaseous helium the intermolecular forces are negligible, while in solid iodine London forces are the only forces and they hold the solid together.

blocks.prompt: II. When the vapour pressure of a liquid equals the external pressure, what phenomenon occurs?
blocks.explanation: The liquid boils at the temperature at which its vapour pressure becomes equal to the external (atmospheric) pressure (5.9).

blocks.prompt: III. When water freezes at 0 °C, its density decreases due to:

options.text: empty spaces present in the structure of ice

blocks.explanation: In ice the hydrogen-bonded water molecules take a regular open tetrahedral arrangement with empty spaces, so ice occupies about 9% more volume and its density decreases (5.4.4).

blocks.prompt: IV. Which of the following options is wrong about hydrides of groups 14, 15, 16, and 17 elements?

options.text: Only H₂O, NH₃ and HF show H-bonding.
The molecules of CH₄ are non-polar.
H₂S is a gas at room temperature but H₂O is liquid.

blocks.explanation: A hydrogen bond needs H joined to a highly electronegative atom (F, O or N) carrying a lone pair (5.4.3). CH₄, H₂S, HCl and similar hydrides do not meet this, so 'all the hydrides show H-bonding' is wrong.

blocks.prompt: V. Which of following is the correct sequence of increasing ∆Hv values of substances mentioned?
blocks.explanation: ∆Hv depends on the strength of intermolecular forces (5.10): H₂O has the most extensive hydrogen bonding (40.6 kJ mol⁻¹), NH₃ weaker hydrogen bonding (21.7 kJ mol⁻¹ in the chapter), and F₂ only weak London forces. So H₂O > NH₃ > F₂, i.e. increasing order F₂ < NH₃ < H₂O.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The question asks for increasing ∆Hv values, but every option is written with '>' (decreasing). The only true statement is (a) H₂O > NH₃ > F₂; written in increasing order it is F₂ < NH₃ < H₂O.

blocks.prompt: VI. Surface tension of a liquid is due to:
blocks.explanation: Molecules at the surface feel a net inward pull from the molecules below them (intermolecular forces), so the surface behaves like a stretched skin (5.5).

blocks.prompt: VII. Amorphous solids:

options.text: undergo clean cleavage when cut with knife
do not have definite geometric shape

blocks.explanation: Amorphous solids (glass, plastic sulphur, charcoal) have no regular three-dimensional geometric shape and no long-range order; they melt over a range of temperature (5.12.2).

blocks.prompt: VIII. Which change of state involves overcoming only London dispersion forces?
blocks.explanation: I₂ molecules are non-polar, so only London forces act between them. Ice and ethanol need hydrogen bonds to be broken; dissolving NaCl breaks ionic bonds.

blocks.prompt: IX. In which of the following substances are London dispersion forces the only significant intermolecular forces present?
blocks.explanation: CH₄ is non-polar and its H is not joined to F, O or N, so only London forces act. NH₃, H₂O and HF form hydrogen bonds.

blocks.prompt: X. Which of the following is a characteristic property of crystalline solids?

options.text: They have a range of melting points.
They have a definite and sharp melting point.
They lack a regular arrangement of particles.

blocks.explanation: Crystalline solids melt sharply at a definite temperature and can be identified by it (5.12.1). They are anisotropic and have regular long-range order; (a), (b) and (d) describe amorphous solids.

blocks.prompt: XI. Which of the following liquids would you expect to have the highest viscosity at a given temperature?
blocks.explanation: Glycerol has three –OH groups per molecule, so it forms very extensive hydrogen bonding; stronger intermolecular forces mean greater viscosity (5.6.1). Diethyl ether has no –OH and the lowest viscosity.

blocks.prompt: XII. Which type of intermolecular force is present in all types of molecule regardless of their polarity?
blocks.explanation: Every molecule has an electron cloud that can form instantaneous dipoles, so London dispersion forces act in all molecules; in non-polar molecules they are the only forces (5.4.1).

blocks.prompt: XIII. Liquid crystals exhibit properties:
blocks.explanation: Liquid crystals flow and show viscosity like liquids, but have parallel ordered arrangement and optical properties like crystals (5.13).

blocks.text: Q.2 Attempt the following short-answer questions:

blocks.prompt: a. Explain, at a molecular level, why evaporation leads to a cooling effect.
blocks.explanation: Only the high-energy molecules escape from the liquid surface, and the low-energy molecules are left behind. So the average kinetic energy, and hence the temperature, of the remaining liquid falls; heat then flows from the surroundings into the liquid, which cools the surroundings too (5.7).

blocks.prompt: b. Explain why liquids with stronger intermolecular forces tend to have lower rates of evaporation at a given temperature compared to liquids with weaker intermolecular forces.
blocks.explanation: To evaporate, a molecule must have enough kinetic energy to overcome the attractions of its neighbours. With stronger forces a higher minimum energy is needed, so a smaller fraction of molecules can escape at that temperature, and the rate of evaporation is lower (e.g. water evaporates more slowly than acetone).

blocks.prompt: c. One feels sense of cooling under the fan after bath.
blocks.explanation: After a bath a film of water stays on the skin. The fan removes the vapour and speeds up evaporation; the escaping high-energy water molecules take their energy from the body, so the skin cools (5.7).

blocks.prompt: d. Dynamic equilibrium is established during evaporation of a liquid in a closed vessel at constant temperature.
blocks.explanation: In a closed vessel the vapour molecules cannot escape; they collect above the liquid and some return to it (condensation). The rate of condensation rises until it equals the rate of evaporation. Then both processes continue at the same rate, so the amount of vapour (vapour pressure) stays constant: liquid ⇌ vapour, a dynamic equilibrium (5.8).

blocks.prompt: e. The boiling point of water is different at Lahore and Murree hills.
blocks.explanation: A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the external pressure. Lahore is at low altitude where the air pressure is about 760 torr, so water boils at about 100 °C. At Murree hills (high altitude) the pressure is about 700 torr, so water boils at about 98 °C (5.9.1).

blocks.prompt: f. Discuss two significant consequences of the lower density of ice compared to liquid water in natural environments.?
blocks.explanation:
1. Ice floats on water, so lakes and seas freeze from the top downwards and not from the bottom.
2. The floating ice blanket insulates the water beneath it from the cold air, so the water below stays liquid and fish and other aquatic life survive under frozen lakes and oceans (5.4.4).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The question ends with a stray '.?' ('environments.?'); only the question mark belongs there.

blocks.prompt: g. Why B.P of a liquid increases when the external pressure rises?
blocks.explanation: A liquid boils when its vapour pressure becomes equal to the external pressure. At a higher external pressure the liquid must be heated more (to a higher temperature) before its vapour pressure reaches that pressure, so the boiling point rises; e.g. water boils at 120 °C at 1489 torr, and food cooks faster in a pressure cooker (5.9.1).

blocks.prompt: h. Mention four items in which liquid crystals are used.
blocks.explanation:
1. Displays (LCDs) of TVs, computer and laptop screens and cell phones.
2. Calculators and watches.
3. Thermometers and temperature sensors (e.g. finding faulty connections on circuit boards).
4. Medical diagnosis: locating tumours (e.g. early breast cancer), which are warmer than nearby tissue (5.13.2).

blocks.prompt: i. How do you differentiate between crystalline solids and amorphous solids?
blocks.explanation: They differ in the order of their particles and hence in shape, melting and directional properties (Table 5.5).

rows: No definite shape; lumps or powder
Melt over a range of temperature

blocks.prompt: j. Propanone (CH₃COCH₃), propanol (CH₃CH₂CH₂OH) and butane (CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃) have very similar relative molecular masses. List them in the expected order of increasing boiling points. Explain your answer.
blocks.explanation:
Order: butane < propanone < propanol.
Butane is non-polar: only weak London forces (b.p. about −0.5 °C).
Propanone is polar (C=O): London plus dipole-dipole forces (b.p. 56 °C).
Propanol has an O–H group: hydrogen bonding, the strongest (b.p. about 97 °C).
With similar masses the London forces are similar, so the extra forces decide the order.

blocks.prompt: k. Discuss how hydrogen bonding is responsible for the relatively high surface tension of water.
blocks.explanation: Each water molecule forms hydrogen bonds with its neighbours. A molecule at the surface has no water molecules above it, so the hydrogen bonds with the molecules below pull it strongly inwards. This strong inward pull makes the surface stretched like a skin; so water has a high surface tension (72.75 × 10⁻³ N m⁻¹ at 20 °C) compared with ethanol (22.75 × 10⁻³) (5.4.4, 5.5).

blocks.prompt:
l. What type of intermolecular forces will dominate in the following liquids?
(i) NH₃ (ii) Ar (iii) CH₃COCH₃ (iv) CH₃OH
blocks.explanation:
(i) NH₃: hydrogen bonding (H joined to N, which has a lone pair).
(ii) Ar: London dispersion forces only (non-polar atoms).
(iii) CH₃COCH₃: dipole-dipole forces (polar C=O; no O–H, so no hydrogen bonding between its own molecules).
(iv) CH₃OH: hydrogen bonding (O–H group).

blocks.prompt:
m. The boiling points and molar masses of hydrides of some first-row elements are tabulated below:
(Table printed: CH₄, boiling point 109 K, molar mass 16 g mol⁻¹; NH₃, 240 K, 17 g mol⁻¹; H₂O, 373 K, 18 g mol⁻¹.)
Suggest reasons for the difference in their boiling points in terms of the type of molecules involved and the nature of the forces present between them.
blocks.explanation:
The molar masses are almost equal, so the London forces are similar; the difference comes from polarity and hydrogen bonding.
CH₄: non-polar molecule, only weak London forces, so lowest b.p. (109 K).
NH₃: polar, hydrogen bonding, but N has only one lone pair, so about one hydrogen bond per molecule and weaker bonds: b.p. 240 K.
H₂O: two H atoms and two lone pairs, so two hydrogen bonds per molecule on average, and O is more electronegative than N: strongest, most extensive hydrogen bonding, highest b.p. (373 K).

blocks.prompt: Q.3. What are London dispersion forces? Give examples, and discuss the factors affecting these forces.
blocks.explanation:
Definition: The momentary force of attraction between an instantaneous dipole and an induced dipole is called instantaneous dipole-induced dipole (id-id) force or London dispersion force.
Origin: electrons keep moving, so at any instant the electron cloud of an atom or molecule may be unevenly distributed, giving a temporary (instantaneous) dipole. This dipole distorts (polarizes) the electron cloud of a neighbouring molecule and induces a dipole in it; the two attract each other. The dipoles keep forming and disappearing.
These are the only forces among non-polar molecules and atoms, and they are present in all molecules.
Examples: noble gases (He, Ne, Ar...), halogens (F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂), hydrocarbons (CH₄, C₂H₆, C₆H₁₄), CCl₄.
Factors:
1. Molecular mass and size: larger atoms and molecules have more electrons and a more easily polarized electron cloud, so stronger forces. Halogens change from gases (F₂, Cl₂) to liquid (Br₂) to solid (I₂, b.p. 458 K); boiling points of noble gases rise from He (4.22 K) to Xe (165 K).
2. Surface area (shape): a longer molecule has more points of contact with its neighbours, so stronger forces. C₂H₆ boils at −88.6 °C but C₆H₁₄ at 68.7 °C. Among the isomers of pentane (same Mr), straight-chain n-pentane has the largest surface area and highest b.p., 2-methylbutane is intermediate, and compact 2,2-dimethylpropane has the lowest.

blocks.prompt: Q.4 Hydrogen bonding is present in H₂O, NH₃, HF, (CH₃)₂CO and CHCl₃ molecules. Sketch structures and discuss briefly.
blocks.explanation:
Condition: a hydrogen bond forms when H is bonded to a highly electronegative atom (F, O, N), so H carries δ+, and it is attracted to a lone pair on F, O or N of a neighbouring molecule. It is shown by a dotted line (…) and is about one tenth as strong as a covalent bond.
1. H₂O: bent molecule, two O–H bonds and two lone pairs on O (Hδ+, Oδ−). Sketch: Oδ−–Hδ+ … :Oδ− of the next molecule. Each molecule forms on average two hydrogen bonds, giving a three-dimensional network; hence high b.p. (100 °C).
2. NH₃: pyramidal, three N–H bonds and one lone pair on N. Sketch: H₂N–H … :NH₃. Only one lone pair, so about one hydrogen bond per molecule and weaker bonding; b.p. −33 °C.
3. HF: H–F with three lone pairs on F, but only one H. Sketch: H–F … H–F … H–F, a zig-zag chain (in the solid). F is the most electronegative, so the bond is strong; b.p. 19.9 °C. Trapping of H between two F atoms makes HF a weak acid.
4. (CH₃)₂CO (propanone) and CHCl₃ (chloroform): neither forms hydrogen bonds with its own kind. Propanone has a polar C=O with lone pairs on O but no O–H; chloroform has a C–H whose H is made δ+ by the three Cl atoms (its own molecules show dipole-dipole forces, 5.4.2). When they are mixed, the H of CHCl₃ is attracted to a lone pair on the O of propanone: Cl₃C–Hδ+ … :O=C(CH₃)₂ (beyond the chapter).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: (CH₃)₂CO and CHCl₃ do not show hydrogen bonding among their own molecules: propanone has no H on O, N or F, and the chapter gives dipole-dipole forces for chloroform (5.4.2). A weak hydrogen bond forms only between a CHCl₃ molecule and a propanone molecule when the two are mixed.

blocks.prompt: Q.5 Discuss the structural changes when water turns into ice. Justify the empty spaces in its crystals as compared to H₂O at 4 °C and lower density of ice.
blocks.explanation:
1. A water molecule has a tetrahedral arrangement around O: two corners hold the O–H bonds and two hold the lone pairs. So each molecule can form hydrogen bonds with four neighbours (two through its H atoms, two through its lone pairs).
2. In liquid water (densest at 4 °C) the hydrogen bonds keep breaking and re-forming, and the molecules move about and pack fairly closely in an irregular way.
3. When water is cooled and freezes, the molecules lose kinetic energy and become fixed. Each O is held tetrahedrally by hydrogen bonds to four other water molecules, and this regular arrangement extends through the whole crystal, forming an open hexagonal cage-like network.
4. Because the hydrogen bonds hold the molecules at fixed distances and angles, they cannot come close together, and empty spaces are left in the network.
5. So ice occupies about 9% more volume than the same mass of water, and its density is lower; ice floats on water.
Consequence: lakes freeze from the top; the floating ice insulates the water below, so aquatic life survives (5.4.4).

blocks.prompt: Q.6 How liquid crystals resemble liquids and solids? Give their uses in daily life.
blocks.explanation:
Liquid crystals: at certain temperatures some substances exist in a phase that is neither fully liquid nor fully solid (crystalline solid → cloudy liquid (liquid crystal) → clear liquid). Their molecules are rigid and rod-like (length four to eight times the diameter).
Resemblance to liquids: they flow like liquids; they show viscosity like liquids; individual molecules can migrate through the fluid.
Resemblance to solids (crystals): they have a parallel ordered arrangement (long axes roughly parallel, like logs in a stack of firewood); they show optical properties like crystals; they are somewhat rigid; they are always anisotropic; molecules can spin about the long axis but cannot rotate end over end.
Uses in daily life:
1. Liquid crystal displays (LCDs): TVs, computer and laptop screens, cell phone displays, calculators, watches, oscillographs (electro-optic devices that modulate light).
2. Diagnostics: cholesteric liquid crystals applied to the skin locate tumours, which are warmer than the surrounding tissue (early detection of breast cancer).
3. Temperature sensing: thermometers and finding faulty connections on circuit boards by their higher temperature (5.13).

blocks.prompt:
Q.7 Describe the following properties of crystalline solids.
i) Geometrical shape ii) Melting point
iii) Cleavage plan iv) Habit of a crystal
blocks.explanation:
i) Geometrical shape: every crystalline solid has a definite, distinctive geometrical shape because its atoms, ions or molecules are arranged in a definite order in three dimensions. The interfacial angles at which the faces meet are always the same for a given crystal, however it is grown, and the faces and angles stay characteristic even in a fine powder.
ii) Melting point: crystalline solids have sharp, definite melting points (all bonds are alike and break at one temperature), so they can be identified by their melting points; amorphous solids melt over a range.
iii) Cleavage plane: when a crystalline solid is broken, it breaks along definite planes called cleavage planes. These planes are inclined to one another at a particular angle for a given crystal, and the angle differs from one solid to another.
iv) Habit of a crystal: the shape in which a crystal usually grows is its habit. If the growing conditions stay the same, the shape stays the same; if conditions change, the shape may change. E.g. NaCl crystals are cubic, but become needle-like when 10% urea is present in the solution as an impurity (5.12.1).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Part iii) is printed 'Cleavage plan'; it means cleavage plane.

blocks.prompt: Q8. A sample of an unknown gas has a mass of 0.560 g. It occupies a volume of 2.87 × 10⁻⁴ m³ at a temperature of 300 K and a pressure of 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa. Calculate the molar mass of the gas. (Gas constant, R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
blocks.explanation:
Given: m = 0.560 g, V = 2.87 × 10⁻⁴ m³, T = 300 K, P = 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa, R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
Required: molar mass M
Formula: PV = (m/M)RT, so M = mRT / PV
Substitution: M = (0.560 g × 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ × 300 K) / (1.01 × 10⁵ Pa × 2.87 × 10⁻⁴ m³)
Numerator = 1396 g J mol⁻¹
Denominator = 28.99 Pa m³ = 28.99 J (1 Pa m³ = 1 J)
M = 1396 / 28.99 g mol⁻¹ = 48.2 g mol⁻¹
Answer: molar mass of the gas = 48.2 g mol⁻¹

blocks.prompt: Q9. In a laboratory experiment, 150 cm³ of a volatile liquid was completely vaporized at 98 °C and a pressure of 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa. The mass of the vapor was found to be 0.495 g. Determine the molecular mass of the liquid (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹).
blocks.explanation:
Given: V = 150 cm³ = 150 × 10⁻⁶ m³ = 1.50 × 10⁻⁴ m³ (volume of the vapour), T = 98 °C + 273 = 371 K, P = 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa, m = 0.495 g, R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
Required: Mr
Formula: Mr = mRT / PV
Substitution: Mr = (0.495 g × 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ × 371 K) / (1.01 × 10⁵ Pa × 1.50 × 10⁻⁴ m³)
Numerator = 1526.8 g J mol⁻¹
Denominator = 15.15 J
Mr = 1526.8 / 15.15 g mol⁻¹ = 100.8 g mol⁻¹
Answer: molecular mass of the liquid ≈ 101 (molar mass 101 g mol⁻¹)
